utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. As I promised yesterday, that -- the Bench has an oral decision on the admission of documents tendered by the Prosecution from the bar table to deliver. On the 1st of June 2005, the Prosecution tendered six documents from the bar table. The Defence filed a motion on 6 June 2005 objecting to the admission of three of those documents. The Prosecution filed its response on the 20th June 2005. Document number 135 is the 1996 OTP statement of Mr. Halilovic and the subject of a separate decision. Documents number 36 and 56 are already admitted into the evidence as exhibits D406 and D273. The Prosecution request is moot in this respect. In its response, the Prosecution withdrew the document number 124 as a proposed exhibit. The Trial Chamber therefore, having considered the arguments of both parties, will decide on the documents number 37 and 85. The Trial Chamber has the responsibility to ensure a fair and expeditious trial, which is conducted in accordance with the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, with due respect for the rights of the accused. The Trial Chamber found that in principle, the appropriate way to introduce evidence is to tender document evidence through witness testimony. However, in accordance with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and the guidelines, the Trial Chamber finds that there is no blanket prohibition on admission of documents simply on the ground that the purported author of the document has not been called to testify. The Trial Chamber notes that the party tendering documents without calling its author, or for that matter any witness who can corroborate the content or comment on the reliability of the document, is running a certain risk. In particular, in so doing, the probative value of the document in question may be diminished, or in some instances, the document may be excluded pursuant to Rule 89(D). As for document number 85, the Trial Chamber notes that this document is a private correspondence between Mr. Halilovic and Izetbegovic which was discussed during the interview of Sefer Halilovic with the Prosecution in 2001. The Trial Chamber has granted the Defence request for certification of the decision to admit the 2001 interview and defers its decision on admission of this document, document number 85, until such time the Appeals Chamber has rendered its decision. The admission of document number 37 is challenged on the basis that it bears insufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity, as the document is unsigned and only bears the name of a deceased individual. The Trial Chamber notes its guidelines in which it's held that the fact that a document is unsigned or unstamped does not a priori render it void of authenticity. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the document bears sufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity. The Trial Chamber finds the document is of relevance and has probative value. The admittance of the document does not infringe upon the right to a fair trial, as the Trial Chamber has already heard evidence in court on the alleged existence of an IKM in Jablanica and on preparations of operation to lift the blockade of Mostar. This piece of evidence supplements the evidence already presented in court. The Trial Chamber reiterates: The admission of a document into evidence is not indication of the weight that may be given to that document and the principle of free evaluation of evidence. Thus, the Trial Chamber admits the document number 37 into evidence. The Registrar is requested to assign an exhibit number to this document. It's so decided. Well, having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Could I just ask you to look at a piece of paper please and read carefully the details that are on that piece of paper. Just read it quietly to yourself. Are the details of your name and your date of birth correctly stated on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that please be shown to the Prosecutor? Thank you. Your Honours, I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think there is any objections from the part of the Prosecution. So it's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D448, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Your Honours, could we please move to the -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Now, in 1992, did you find yourself imprisoned by forces of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you explain how long you were kept imprisoned on this first occasion in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: For about two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And ultimately, did that period of imprisonment come to an end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And after that, were you imprisoned a second time by HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: If I may just clarify one thing, the first time I was imprisoned was when a clash broke out between the HVO and the BH army, and all Bosniak men of military age, all able-bodied men were detained in schools and hangars in Prozor so this same applied to me, and so much about the first time I was imprisoned. The second time it happened occurred in June 1993. Much like the first time. The entire population was detained and here I mean the male persons aged between 18 and 60. Later on in August we were all expelled. I was among the first to be detained in June and I was eventually released about 20 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And after being released from that particular custody, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was still dangerous to remain in town. Some of my colleagues had been killed. I fled. The reason I'm using that term is Prozor was surrounded so you couldn't just leave. I took a path through the woods to flee. I joined another group and eventually reached an area controlled by the BH army which we used to refer to as the free territory. My only aim was to save my skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When you reached the free territory, which particular army unit did you encounter there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The Prozor Independent Battalion was there. I knew most of the people who were part of it. Most of them at the battalion command were my former students and pupils. They asked me to remain with them and as I had no other solution at the time, no other accommodation, I agreed to stay. I didn't have any particular tasks that I was assigned at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could I just ask you before I come to the way your tasks developed, did you have any military expertise or any military background of your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, when you arrived at the Prozor Independent Battalion, what tasks did you initially take up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I had no specific tasks. It was by coincidence that I ended up there. But many people knew me and they proposed that I liaise between the civilian authorities, the War Presidency of Prozor, based in Jablanica at the time, on the one hand, and the Prozor Battalion on the other. These were no clear-cut assignments. I was merely to coordinate issues as they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I just have some questions about some personnel at the Independent Prozor Battalion at that time. Firstly, when you arrived there, who was the commander of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Enver Buza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was Enver Buza a local person or did he come from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: He came from somewhere else. This was the first time I saw him. I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did you learn where it was that he came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Later on, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: From Visoko, which is a town near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And at the time when you arrived there, who was, to the best of your recollection, who was the deputy commander to Enver Buza in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I believe Mustafa Hero. I knew him too because he had once been a pupil of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you recall who was officially the military security officer of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Mustafa Bektas. He was another person I knew, a former pupil of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And who was the officer in charge of counterintelligence and intelligence gathering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I didn't understand much about the military hierarchy. As far as I know, it was Erzimana Dzogic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could you just explain to the Judges here how your role developed and what role you came to play in the Independent Prozor Battalion and its command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours perhaps before the witness answers that I might ask that we move to the private session as those answers might have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, in which corps structure was the Prozor Independent Battalion, in the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The 6th. The 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And during the combat operations, including those at Uzdol, on the 14th of September 1993, in which military structure was the Prozor Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Salko Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you recall who his deputy was at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you recall any other officers from the command of the 6th Corps who came to your area of operations in the time that you were present and who you came to know by sight or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Most frequently, person who was in touch with us was a man named Fazlic. I'm not sure about his first name. We called him Braco. He was from the 6th Corps. I'm not sure if he was a deputy of sorts. I'm not sure about his precise position. I know he was an officer serving with the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before we come to the combat operations themselves, I just want to ask you some questions about the information available to you about the collection of hamlets and small villages known as Uzdol. Now, in general terms, in late August and early September of 1993, what did you and those you worked with at the Independent Prozor Battalion know about the military situation in the hamlets in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We knew a good deal. Many of the Bosniaks it would had remained in Prozor had been taken trench-digging in the Uzdol area. Some of them managed to escape and as soon as they reached the independent Battalion we would take statements from them which helped us to put together a picture of what was going on, what sort of weapons were available and who specifically was in the village. I think we had a pretty clear picture of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And perhaps just in your own words, could you explain to the Judges, what was that picture that you had of what was going on in Uzdol at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: You mean during combat or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I will come to combat later on but at the moment, what information you had about the setup effectively within Uzdol and its small villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We knew that at the elementary school building there was a rather large group of soldiers. Further, we knew that there were very few women and children left there. For the most part, following the first clash in October 1992, they left Prozor and moved into Bosniak flats. Those who remained in Uzdol were for the most part men. Sometimes when the situation appeared to be safe, some women and children would also come over. We also knew that each house had at least one barrel, that is weapon, and sometimes more. What we were positive about is that each house in the village was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And -- pardon me -- did you have any information as to whether the soldiers in the village were always wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: For the most part, but there were those who weren't. The reason probably being they were short of uniforms. But they did is have a lot of weapons. There were a lot of people in the village who did guard duty, and once their shift was done, they would simply go back home. Therefore, some were in uniform and some were in plain clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Were you aware of the existence -- you've mentioned the school building there in evidence. Were you aware of whether that school building was functioning as a school at that time or whether it had some other function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was just for military purposes, and part of it was used for soldiers, for Bosniaks, who were fortifying the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And by soldiers who were Bosniaks, do you mean -- I should ask you are you talking about prisoners or are you talking about Bosniaks fighting on the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I mean the Bosniaks, the civilians, who remained in Prozor and were detained in a number of different schools throughout Prozor, without mentioning the specific hamlets, Uzdol being one of the latter. Those were Bosniak civilians who had been brought over from Prozor to the school at Uzdol and used as a labour force whilst detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And just finally -- perhaps I won't go to that question. I now want to move to the leadup to the fighting which happened in Uzdol on the 14th of September in 1993. Can you say how long was it before that battle in time that you first learned of the possibility of widespread offensive activities, offensive military activities, in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Perhaps about 10 days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And what was the first that you learned of the possibility of such activities? Just explain to the Court what happened in your unit or neighbouring units or generally speaking that alerted to you the possibility that such a thing might happen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: First of all, a unit came. I think they were part of the 45th Brigade, but I wasn't certain. Our conclusion was that something was in the offing, given that they were there to give us a hand. That was my first impression on seeing them arrive in the Dobro Polje area where our command was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you see Sefer Halilovic at some stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Roughly, at about the same time, we were shelled by multiple rocket launchers. The shelling became more frequent, heavier than usual and we were wondering about the reason, was this some sort of attack or what? It was then that I found out that Sefer Halilovic had arrived and that they were the ones being targeted, and that's why the shelling had grown in intensity. I think it was that same day or the next day that I saw him. He came outside the headquarters to greet the soldiers. He was exceptionally popular among the troops. He was greeted exuberantly, with a huge applause. He greeted the soldiers. He spoke briefly and quite formally. He said that he was hoping we would overcome these present difficulties and that we would eventually make it and survive. It was something along those lines but it was nothing really substantial that I could remember verbatim right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you remember whether on that first occasion there was any discussion of specific combat activities or was it simply general comments of the type you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: My impression was this was a group of officers who were there to sort things. That's what I believed they were, an inspection team that had arrived to bring more order to these military units and sort out a number of things. A day or two later, however, Erzimana and myself, the two of us were collecting intelligence, were invited to come to a meeting and talk about whatever information we had gathered. Once questions started being thrown at us, I realised that an operation was in the offing but I still didn't know what specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. That second meeting that you've referred to, can you tell the Court where that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before that's answered, I apologise for objecting -- for rising at this point. I couldn't object during the last answer because it would have involved interrupting the witness and the translation. The Prosecution objects to the answer, that the witness has answered that his impression was that it was a group of officers and that an inspection team that had arrived to bring more order. The Prosecution objects to that answer unless the witness can first lay the foundation, the basis of his knowledge to give that answer. It wasn't in the question so it was just hard to object while the answer was being given. So perhaps that could be clarified before we go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's very strange to object to the answer from a witness rather than the question. If you have some doubts on that issue, you may raise it during the cross-examination. Or if Mr. Morrissey is kind enough to clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I indicate that in due course I'll ask some questions about what was the basis for the witness's belief and impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Just excuse me while I locate the question. Okay. You indicated a second meeting where you yourself and Erzimana attended and I wanted to ask you where did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In Dobro Polje in the building of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And on that occasion, can you recall how long yourself and Erzimana were present answering questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: A maximum of ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And can you recall what was the focus of the questions that you were being asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they were mostly interested in the positions of artillery pieces, tanks, in the area of Makljen, Crni Vrh, number of troops and along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now I just want to ask you about the personnel who were present to the best of your recollection at that meeting, whether it be from the inspection team or from a corps commands or anywhere in fact. What is the best you can recall about the people who were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can't enumerate with any certainty who was present at the meeting. I remember some people, though. I remember that Fazlic was there, as was Gusic, Buza. I don't remember seeing Sefer at the meeting. It was possible that he was there. Perhaps someone may correct me if I'm wrong. Cikotic was there. I don't remember his first name. I think that Karic was there. However, I saw those people for the first time there. Therefore, I'm not entirely sure whether what I'm telling you is completely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just ask you this? You mentioned that Sefer Halilovic came with some other officers and now you've mentioned Karic. Can you remember the names of any other officers who were associated with Sefer Halilovic in that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. I don't remember. I know that they arrived in a jeep. I think that there were four of them. It could have been his brother who was there. I know that his son was with him and I think that Karic was there as well, and as for the others, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Just to jump forward -- no, I won't jump forward. We will go chronologically through. Okay, thank you for that. This meeting at Dobro Polje that you've mentioned, can you say approximately how long before the combat operations on the 14th of September did the Dobro Polje meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Perhaps seven to eight days prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I must reiterate that I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll ask you the questions and see what happens. Do you recall whether or not any journalists were present in the company of Sefer Halilovic on the occasions when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: There was a journalist there. I don't know whether he was in the company of Sefer Halilovic, however. He was there talking to people, interviewing them. I talked to him myself. I'm not sure what it was about but I know that he interviewed some soldiers, took some photographs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you recall that person's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think that his name was Semso or something similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And do you recall his second name or his family name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: If someone were to remind me. I used to know that last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not allowed to remind you so I won't. We will just move on to another topic. Very well. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Could it have been Omerovic or something similar to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll just move on to another topic. The -- did you observe Sefer Halilovic on any occasion to meet with the commander of the Independent Prozor Battalion, Enver Buza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I saw him once. It could have been the 13th. Actually, our battalion had a task which it did not accomplish. I am not sure what task it was exactly, but I remember Sefer coming and asking Buza how come he didn't do what he had been ordered to do, and then Buza explained the reasons for not accomplishing the task. So it was then that I saw him talking to Buza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And could you just briefly explain to the Judges here, now that we've raised this meeting, how did that meeting proceed and what happened after it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question. You mean the meeting between Sefer and Buza or the meeting of the command?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I mean the meeting between Sefer and Buza. We will go back to the meeting of the command but right now since we've raised it, could you just explain how the meeting between Sefer and Buza developed and what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. Sefer demanded that Buza act in accordance with the order. Buza went into justifying all that and their discussion was quite stern. I remember Sefer saying that Buza would be held accountable for failing to accomplish the task. However, that he would postpone dealing with that until everything was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Which order did -- was Buza supposed to have obeyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't know whose order it was. We mostly received orders from the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were you familiar with any order that you received from any other body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Now, I just want to ask you, you mentioned earlier on that you had an impression of what the role of Sefer Halilovic was and I just want to ask you, based on your observations of the days leading up to combat, what did you base that impression on? What did you see that gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question? I'm not sure what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier on, you indicated that you had the impression that Sefer and the inspection team had come to sort things out in the area. Can you indicate what it was that you based that impression on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I was not quite focused there for a while. That's why I asked you to repeat the question. Now, as for that impression of mine, I remember exactly how I came to have that impression. When I came to the area where the battalion was, I had a completely different impression before reaching the area. I thought that this was the real army. However, once I got there, I saw that half of them were civilians and half of them were soldiers who practically did not carry out their duties. It looked very unorganised to me. The others kept repeating the same and saying that military experts were needed to come in and take care of that because practically none of the soldiers were professional soldiers. They all acted on their own, and it was just that the circumstances dictated that. We had no other way of defending ourselves, of saving our lives. Therefore it was my impression that somebody else would arrive, who had military knowledge and expertise and who help us bring things into order. This is why I thought that this team was precisely the team which was supposed to come in and put everything in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, just to pursue that a little bit further. When you escaped from Prozor or fled from Prozor, at that time, what was your understanding of the position in -- of Sefer Halilovic within the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The entire time I believed him to be the commander. When I saw him in Dobro Polje I was still under the impression he was commander. I did not have information to the contrary. Later on I learned that it was otherwise. I knew him from television. In the beginning of the war I saw him appear on television several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You've indicated that he seemed very popular with the soldiers. Can you say how his relations appeared to be with the officers, and after -- and then after that I'll ask you how his relations seemed to be with Buza in particular. But can you say how his relations seemed to be with the officers generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to witness his meeting with other officers. I could have only seen something in passing. Therefore I had nothing to establish solid judgement. However, just before the operation began, it was my impression that he did not enjoy a great deal of authority among the officers. That was my impression and it was something that surprised me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And what do you say about his relations with Enver Buza at that time, in terms of what you observed yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was my impression that the animosity that existed between them had its roots in the past. Perhaps there was something between them that had happened earlier. However, I did not have any more detailed information about what it was. If there was anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Thank you. Now, we will just move on to the preparations for combat now and the launching of the combat activities. On the 13th of September, that is, the day before the Independent Prozor Battalion ultimately went into battle, were you aware of any combat on your right flank in the region of Crni Vrh and Makljen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And at that time, what was your understanding of the role that the Prozor Independent Battalion was supposed to play?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did not know the exact role of the battalion. However, I spoke to Buza, to Erzimana. Buza said to me that our task was set in detail in the order. That night, when our battalion was supposed to set out, Buza was awaiting something. He explained to us that he didn't have fuel. Erzimana and I were waiting for the fuel the entire night, in order for the battalion to set out, as ordered. However, he did not explain to me in detail what the task of the battalion was. In the morning, on the 13th, I learned that the 4th company of the battalion was supposed to go into action with the troops on the right side. I think it was the Vakuf brigade. They were supposed to go to Crni Vrh where the main HVO artillery was positioned and their task was to destroy it, to neutralise it. This is how I know that there was combat there and that we were dissatisfied with how it all progressed, because the guides who were supposed to lead the troops were people who were not from the area. They didn't know the terrain, and this is why this company came upon a minefield and there were a lot of casualties. That was quite a great disappointment for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've indicated that at some stage on the 13th, Sefer Halilovic arrived and had a talk with Buza and I'd just like to ask you what's the approximate time that Halilovic arrived on that day, the 13th, and spoke to Buza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think it was in the afternoon or in the evening. It could have been at around 6 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. After the meeting or the -- after the meeting between Sefer Halilovic and Buza, did anyone remain behind with Buza after Sefer left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean did anyone remain with Buza? I was there in the vicinity. I talked to him. But not about the topic of his conversation with Sefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. The question was a little bit of an awkward one, Witness, so I'll try it another way. Did Sefer leave anyone behind from his own group, from the inspection team, with Buza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't remember that there was anyone there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just before we go on, could we clarify where that occurred? I'm confused as to whether it's the meeting at Dobro Polje or a different meeting, and if so where they had the meeting. My submission if would certainly assist the Trial Chamber's understanding of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course I'm going to ask the question of where it took place. As to whether it's the Dobro Polje meeting, it clearly isn't because the witness has said when the other one was. Just let me proceed with those questions for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you just indicate to clarify that matter, where was this meeting where Sefer met with Buza on the 13th at around 6.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In Dobro Polje, at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, after that, did the troops in fact go into battle on the following day? Or the following morning, I should say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The troops set out in the evening. I'm not sure exactly what time it was but it was quite late in the evening. They were supposed to assemble in a place near the Here village at around 2.00 or perhaps 2.30 in the morning on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you accompany those troops into battle or did you stay somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I remained in the building of the command headquarters in Dobro Polje. However, in the meantime, I took in a car a nurse and another lady who might have been a doctor or a nurse as well, to the place where the troops had assembled and then I went back to the command headquarters in Dobro Polje. I saw the troops assembled there. This is how I know what time it was, around 2 or 2.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I understand. Before we go to what happened the next day, can I just ask you this: Did you see Sefer Halilovic again after that meeting with Buza on that part of the front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think that after that, I did not see Sefer again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you see Vehbija Karic or any other people from the inspection team in that section of the front after the battle at Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I saw only Suljevic. I might have seen someone else too. However, since I didn't know these people very well, I really can't claim with certainty whether any of them was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did you see Suljevic before or during or after the battle at Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Afterwards, upon his return. He was at a command post. I know that based on a conversation with Erzimana, because she had been together with him. She, Suljevic and he were together at that command post. I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And can you say which day it was that you saw Suljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That could have been on the 14th, because this is when I saw Buza and Erzimana and other soldiers who had returned from combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. Now I want to turn now to the 14th and the events of that day. You've indicated you didn't go into battle. Who was the -- who was the first soldier that you saw? Or first of all I should ask you generally. Did you see soldiers after the battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I saw a lot of soldiers. The first one I saw was Osman Hero. He used to help me with some things. He worked quite a lot with me. And he was the first one to tell me about his impressions, because he had participated. I think that he was a company commander or something similar to that. However, it wasn't only him. I talked to many others, and I reiterate that most of them were my former students who had a great deal of respect for me, and would gladly talk to me if I approached them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you ultimately come to take any statements from any of the soldiers of the Prozor Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to this. This is leading. There is a way of getting to this, lay the foundation. This is putting words in the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may establish that step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Your Honours we will establish it step by step.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The first contact was initiated by my curiosity to learn about what had happened. This is how I came to speak to Osman. And Osman also had a need to tell me about what had happened. And I simply noted that down. I would typically note things down, not in a very formal way. But I would note that down. However, after about an hour or two, I entered the office where Erzimana typically worked, and I found her there taking statements from Hero and another man whose name I can't remember. I think it was Jusuf. Then I asked her what's going on? And she said, well, we have to take statements. We have been asked to draft a report. And then she said now that you're here, let's do this together. Therefore, I stayed there, taking the statements. I also noted things down. I never inquired who it was who asked -- who had asked us to do that, but I reasoned with myself that that if it was somebody, it ought to have been the 6th Corps. Therefore, we continued taking statements which we believed to be relevant. At the same time, Buza asked me to take part in that as well, together with Erzimana and Bektas saying that he had been asked to write a report about what had happened and that we ought to do it as fast as possible. Therefore, I saw this as a task that we had been given to draft a report about what had happened, and we did it. We wrote up a report and forwarded it to the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could I just ask, please, that the witness be shown a document, it's Exhibit 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness J, the computer screen is about to show you a document and when it's up on the screen I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This is document 2185, the one that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's okay. We've got a number of different numbering systems here so... Do you see that -- do you have on the screen in front of you now a document with, in the top right-hand corner, the handwritten figures, D476? I'm sorry, perhaps I've got the English copy. Just excuse me a moment. Could I just confirm what the numbers are that you have at the top of your document. Is it DD002185? I'm sorry, Witness, I just need to confirm what document you have in front of you. Do you have in front of you now a document with the numbers at the top, DD002185?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Can I just ask whether that appears to you to be a combat report, a commander's report, which is under the hand of Enver Buza, the commander of the Independent Prozor Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't remember the entire document but I know there was a report like this because I was one of the people who compiled it. It's not that I necessarily recognise my own style, but I probably did have a hand in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If you just excuse me, I'm just going to take you to a couple of aspects of that document and ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, maybe we could have a break before you go into details of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honours, I didn't notice the time. We can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will take a break and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours could I just point out one matter before we start with the questioning? It was brought to my attention that during the course of questions, that I made a slip in -- concerning the protective measures here and I think I should just mention this in open court, that there is the ability for any slip like that to be redacted and edited out so that a slip by a silly barrister does not cause trouble because it's edited at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that we already have it redacted already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I acknowledge my prior history in this regard. Your Honours, could I just ask that the Court deputy provide a paper copy of the order currently being analysed to the witness? It may be a little easier for him to refer to in hard copy. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Just before the break, we looked at this document and you indicated that you may have or that you probably did have a hand in drafting this but that you couldn't remember it precisely. I bear that in mind but I'm just going to ask you to clarify some of the information in it, if I can. First of all, do you see in the first line of the text that the document says, "Pursuant to attack order operative number 01/1500-27 of 11 September 1993"? Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Can you remember now that order, 01/1500-27 of 11 September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. Not by just looking at the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I'll come back to that and show you another document a bit later on. Could you just notice here that the text says, "The Prozor Independent Battalion units infiltrated deep into the enemy territory as planned in the night between 13 and 14 September 1993." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Does that accord with your memory of events, in particular those dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I now have a question about the geography of the area. In the next -- in the next passage, it says, "In another direction, two platoons were infiltrated into the Klupa section and the Blace village sector." I just want to ask you about where Blace and Klupa are located. Can you remember where those places are located? Klupa are located. Can you remember where those places are located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I do remember, none too accurately though. I have a vague idea where these places are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I ask you this? Are they on the main part of the front of the Uzdol -- sorry of the Prozor Independent Battalion, or were they to the right-hand side in the Crni Vrh area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think more to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks. In the next paragraph, the report sets out which units participated in the attack. And you'll see that among the units that are specified there, it says that part of the Prozor MUP forces took part. Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can't find that. Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You'll see there is a sentence beginning, like this, "The following units participated in the attack."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Could you explain to the Judges in general terms how it was that police units, and by which I mean MUP police units, would fight in actions alongside the Prozor Independent Battalion? How would it be arranged and what would happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, near the battalion command there was a unit of civilian police made up of about seven or eight persons. They would be called in in critical situations. According to what I remember they would always find some excuse to not go because they were obeying a different chain of command and I can't specifically remember that they were involved in this action as a MUP unit. Maybe some of them volunteered, individuals. But my memory is not particularly accurate in relation to these events, whether any of them took part or not. I'm talking about their general position, the position they would take whenever it would boil down to joining the battalion in a number of critical situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, it was the general question I was asking you and thank you for that. Now, could we look further down the page to a passage that begins like this: "The armed soldiers and civilians in the surrounded villages even held armed women in front of themselves and started to put up resistance. Fire was returned. The entire Uzdol, Here, Klupa and Scipe sector was under heavy artillery fire." Do you see that paragraph there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you whether that is consistent or not consistent with the information that you were given when you spoke to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think that's the questions about that particular document that I have. No, there is one other question that I have. You've seen the conclusion part of that. You'll see at the conclusion it says that -- perhaps this might be six lines from the bottom. It says, "By my estimate about 65 Croatian soldiers and about 30 civilians mostly armed, were liquidated during the operation. One should bear in mind that the Ustasha artillery was literally destroying the entire Uzdol sector the whole time." Now, do you see that passage there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Could I just ask you whether that is consistent or not consistent with the information that you received from the soldiers that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to this. There is no information before the Trial Chamber at all about him receiving any information from any soldiers at any point about anything. He said he took some statements on all -- or participated in taking statements an hour or two after the soldiers arrived back on the 14th. Now, what anyone told him and when is not in evidence at the moment. My friend is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think before that the witness talked to somebody, maybe Mr. Morrissey could give us some guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think -- I won't make any comments about these objections. I'll just deal with the question another way. Perhaps I could finish with this document which is what I wish to do now and then -- but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, could I -- I'll persist with that question, if I might, Your Honour. I'm going to of course ask him, and I make it quite clear that the reason he's being called, I'm going to ask him about what he knew about alleged atrocities of various sorts and what was done about those. And I'm going to ask him in detail about what actions he took, who took an interest in those. I can assure the Prosecutors I will go through it very thoroughly. At the moment I'm in this document here. If the Prosecutor wishes to object to me putting that before I've laid those, I'll put this document aside and I'll come back to that document later on. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is precisely my objection. He's putting the end proposition before my learned friend asks the leadup questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll accommodate the Prosecution in that regard. We will deal with the matter differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll put it very generally and we will start from there. We'll set this document aside now for a moment, Mr. Witness J, and we will come to the general propositions. Did you become aware that there were allegations of atrocities of --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no. I object. I object to this. The witness is here to give evidence. He's not hear for Mr. Morrissey to put words in the witness's mouth. What we have so far is the witness taking statements or participating in statements being taken an hour or two after the soldiers arrived back. The appropriate question is why did you take the statements? Not to put suggestions to the witness about why he was doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could start with the conversation of this witness with other soldiers, as well as the statement they were taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that objection in my submission is absolutely meritless and is an attempt to derail the proceedings. I'm entitled to lead evidence in the appropriate way and I submit I'm entitled to ask him the general question first and then ask him what he did about these things. That's completely the right way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's start with the statement and the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You've indicated you had some conversations with soldiers immediately after the battle for your own purposes. Could I ask you now: Did you also come to take some statements from those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: My apologies. I wasn't focused there for a moment and I didn't really follow your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's okay. We'll start it again. Did you ever take statements from soldiers of the Independent Prozor Battalion concerning with their actions in the village and any potential atrocities committed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. How many such statements, approximately, did you take from these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It's difficult to remember. Maybe about 15 statements in writing but I must have talked to at least 50 different persons. Perhaps more, perhaps about a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And over what time period did you take those statements and talk to those people? Was it a matter of minutes, hours, days? Approximately how long did it take to speak to the hundred or so and take the 15 or so written statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This may have gone on for ten, 15 days, perhaps even longer. I talked to people whenever I could. Sometimes I met people by accident, through no design of my own. Sometimes I met people in passing. It wasn't a statement-taking process in the strict sense of the word, of someone being called to an office to give a statement. It was a matter of different people's accounts, who was where and who did what, partly out of curiosity and partly because I needed to put together a coherent picture of what exactly had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You mentioned that yourself and Erzimana took part in this process and I want to ask you, which, if any, persons from other organisations appeared to take an interest in this investigation, from the battalion level, from the corps level, from any other level that you recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, the main thing is Buza, the commander, gave us assignments. He was the one who relayed assignments to us. I can't remember whether we had received a request directly from the 6th Corps security, but while talking to people from the 6th Corps, they would always tell us, "Come on, please, get this done. We are getting a lot of heat from Sarajevo to compiling this report and have it delivered." In practical terms this was an assignment for us and also we had to deal with it as swiftly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, just to deal with some aspects of that answer, who were the people from the 6th Corps that you're referring to who said, "Come on, please get this done, we are getting a lot of heat from Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: For the most part, this was Nermin Eminovic and there were people who came with him, Barba most usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you say how frequently Nermin Eminovic made those inquiries -- or perhaps before I ask you the question of how frequently, did he make those inquiries in person, or via the Paket system or radio or a combination of those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was a combination of all these. I myself was in the 6th Corps command building in Konjic once or twice. I saw him then. He would also come to the battalion area, so that was when I saw him. But I believe most frequently contact was established through radio communications and packet Paket communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you remember when was the first contact you had with Nermin after the Uzdol battle itself took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically, but it may have been within days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Can you remember what it was that Nermin said to you on the first occasion when you spoke to him concerning this matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can remember specifically, but the general meaning was that this report had to be drafted as soon as possible because he himself was duty bound to pass it on. The report was also to be as thorough and as extensive and as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did he mention by name who it was in Sarajevo that he was obliged to pass this report on to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Even if he'd mentioned a name, I'm not sure I'd recall the name. In Sarajevo, when we spoke about the main command, the main headquarters and the security, we used these terms to refer to the overall organisation of both the civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Since you've mentioned the civilian authorities, did the civilian authorities appear to you to have any involvement or interest in this matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I think this is an illustration of them actually being familiar with the details. I was a delegate to the Bosnian congress in Sarajevo. I was a member of a delegation that was received by the then president, Alija Izetbegovic, and his deputy, Ejup Ganic. They received us. We were there on another business. We were there to get some information, well not that it matters now what our reasons were being there was but what Izetbegovic told us was before you start saying anything else, please give us a firsthand account of what exactly happened in Uzdol. I gave them my story, the story that I had pieced together thanks to my own investigations. He then asked me a series of questions based on which I concluded that he was well familiar with details and that he had been previously informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I'm just want to go back to the story that you did piece together about this and then I'll ask you what your sources were and how you pieced it together. Could you just explain to the Tribunal and the Judges here what is the story that you pieced together, having performed the functions that you did perform, about what happened in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: After all the interviews that I conducted, I felt almost as if I'd been there myself. Everyone told me about their own experiences, about where specifically they were. I used to know the village from earlier on. I knew what the physical layout of the village was. So I pieced together a picture which I believe faithfully reflects what actually happened. Also based on what people told me. Roughly speaking, this would be as follows. Their intention was to surround the school building where the intervention unit was billeted. They called on them to surrender. They even arrested one person who walked ahead of everyone else, in order to call on the remaining persons there to surrender. This person was killed and then panic ensued. There was random shooting at once and everyone started running in order to take cover. They would run straight through the houses because that was the shortest route out of the village. They were being shot at and they themselves were shooting at others. There was a lot of random shooting. They weren't sure if they had actually hit anyone but they even threw hand grenades. Well, they did whatever they could in order to get away. So the image that I was left with is a chaotic scene of people running for their lives all through the village. That was my conclusion. People were adamant that it should be established whether a crime had occurred or not, and it was much discussed throughout the country by the public. It was difficult to say whether there was a crime or not. I knew for a fact that some people were killed but there was no way I could have concluded specifically about the number of the respective groups that were killed, military officers or civilians. I knew that civilians had been killed too because they said it too, someone had launched a hand grenade and well, someone got killed. So my general idea what occurred was people were just running for their lives and I don't think it would have been possible to actually commit a crime against the civilian population, which is the possibility that was bandied about later on. I don't think that would have been possible. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to ask you some specific matters of the -- concerning the information that you got from the soldiers. Was the topic of any small children being killed raised with you by any of those soldiers -- I shouldn't say the topic. I should ask you a more direct question. Did any soldiers indicate whether or not they knew of small children being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We didn't know. I can say that much. We didn't know that any children had been killed. (redacted) told me that he had thrown a hand grenade into a house because they had been shooting at him from that house. He was very downcast the day he came to see me and this was the first information I got on any children actually being around. He thought there were children in the house, but he didn't have any idea what the result was of that hand grenade being thrown. Why was I under the impression that no such crime was committed, as was widely believed? We intercepted their radio communication, this radio officer of ours, and we had a rough idea of what was going on on their side. They were seized by panic as soon as the shooting started. This was something that I could notice. Based on what was going on at the communications centre and the sort of conversation that they were having, the skirmish probably took a brief while and then the soldiers from our battalion started to run for it. However, the soldiers from the village were thinking throughout that the whole thing was already over and probably they had already informed the neighbouring villages where the artillery positions were. I remember us listening to this closely and there was an officer from the communications centre in the village of Uzdol who used the communications equipment to call a mate who was at a different position. He was swearing at him, he said stop the bloody shelling. You've killed more than ten of our men. I'm not sure if he said ten but he did give a figure. He said, you've already killed more than ten of our men. Stop this thing. And this went on for over half an hour. So that any civilians or soldiers who were killed in this shelling were probably part of the total that was calculated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just ask you a question now. First of all, are you able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps could we just move to the private session for this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, apart from the talking with soldiers and the statements that have been mentioned in evidence here, was it possible for you or anyone else for that matter, to go to Uzdol and see for yourself anything that might be available to look at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. Impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And were you in a position, or did you feel yourself to be in a position at the time, to ask local HVO commanders for permission to go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Had we asked for that, permission probably would not have been granted because any type of contact was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the radio station called Radio Rama?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And where was Radio Rama based in those days? By which I mean September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't know the exact location, but somewhere in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were you familiar with any of the persons who provided news and information over the airwaves from that radio station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just go into of the private session ones again, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go back to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So in terms of the inquiries that you made, you've indicated what they were. Can I ask you now, when you provided the account that you did -- perhaps I'll take a step back from that. You just indicated before that you spoke in fact to the president, Alija Izetbegovic, about that. Can you say approximately when that took place? Was it a matter of weeks after the event or months after it? Which month did the assembly take place which you were in Sarajevo to attend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: End of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. When you were in Sarajevo at the end of September and you met with Izetbegovic and Ganic, what response did Izetbegovic give when you explained the view that you had pieced together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: As I have explained to you, as I've explained to him, what my impression was, he put some questions and then he made a comment to Ganic, saying, "See what they did to us?" I'm not sure whether those were verbatim his words but what he said was along the lines of, "See how they set it up to make it look like a crime?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you ever -- did you ever report to or were you ever instructed to report to, a man called Namik Dzankovic concerning these matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. I remember the name, but I don't know who the person is. Nor did I have any contact, closer contact, with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was it ever suggested to you at the time that you should advise Sefer Halilovic about the investigation that you were performing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. I never heard him mentioned in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I just want you to remember as best you can how it was that the -- that the written statements were compiled over the days that you've indicated that they were. Was it a question of you going into the field and speaking to soldiers or did you ask them to come and meet you somewhere? How was that done? Or was it different in each different case? Perhaps you just explain to the Judges how it unfolded, how it happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Initially, the conversations took place either on an individual basis or within a group, and whenever it was believed that one of the persons could provide an interesting piece of information, that person would be invited to come to the office and then that conversation was taped. There were also such cases where somebody would come in and recommend that we talk to such-and-such person because that person knew some details, and in that case we would follow the advice, talk to that person and note the conversation down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from the ones -- I'm going to come to the details of the tapes in a minute. But apart from the ones that were taped, you indicated that you spoke to quite a large number of soldiers. Did you take any notes of those conversations with the large number of soldiers, I think you said up to 100 but I won't put figures in your mouth. Were there written notes taken of those conversations in any form?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Mostly yes. Sometimes in entirety and sometimes I would simply note down the most important bits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, after the -- perhaps I'll turn to the ones that were taped. When they were taped, what would be done with the tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: There was a misunderstanding. I did not say that I taped the conversations on tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, pardon me. You indicated -- sorry, that's how it was translated through. But perhaps you could just explain what happened with the 15 or so ones where you said a formal statement was taken. How was that recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think that there was a misunderstanding in the term used. I recorded it by hand, in a notebook. Based on all of those statements we compiled a report that was typed up and then sent via Paket communication to the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And to whom at the 6th Corps was that sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly to whom in the 6th Corps these documents were sent. However, based on what I was able to see later, everything was sent to the security sector. That means that my documents were most likely also sent to the security centre. Now, whether the commander did the same, whether he used the same procedure with the documents he received from us, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And just in terms of those records, when did you leave the Prozor Independent Battalion? Or approximately when did you leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Approximately in March of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And without going into detail about this, did you leave -- did you go elsewhere within Bosnia or did you leave the country altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In Bosnia. I went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And who was your -- who was the person who came after you in your position at the Prozor Independent Battalion -- well, perhaps could we go to the private session for this answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the witness please just be given a hard copy of this in the Bosnian language? We will continue to use the E-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Now, what's being shown to you is an order dated the 11th of September which is a combat order from the 6th Corps with a particular order number on it, that being 01/1500-27. I would just like you to look at that document briefly. I want to ask: Did you see that document in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This text looks familiar to me. I suppose that I saw this somewhere. I don't know where. But possibly it was at the commander's desk, because I was with him in the office very often, and he would leaf through the documents in front of him. The text is familiar and I think that I saw it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I now ask that the witness be shown another document. This one is Exhibit 158. I'll provide a copy again for -- Your Honours, what the witness is being shown here is an order dated 15th of the 9th, with an identifying number on it, which is 21 -- you'll see Your Honours it's at the top left-hand corner strictly confidential, number 21-1 and it's dated 15 September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So now in front of you there is an order, it's an exhibit in this trial, an order dated at Voljevac on the 15th of September 1993, so the day after the combat operations in Uzdol. It has a number strictly confidential number 21-1, and it's under the typewritten name of Sefer Halilovic, but has the signature of Karic underneath it. Now, my question to you first of all is this: Before you came to The Hague for these proceedings, had you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did your duties in fact require you to see any orders written by Sefer Halilovic or Vehbija Karic for that matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. This was not typical for some of the assistants to analyse anything. The only way I could see something was if I happened to sit in commander's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'd like the witness now to be shown another document, and this is document 124 -- Exhibit, sorry, 124 and we'll now provide you with another document which I'll ask the same questions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you have before you now a document like the other document, dated the 15th of September 1993 at Voljevac and like the other document, having the document number on the top left-hand corner, 21-1, this time with a signature of Sefer Halilovic on it? Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As with the last document, could I just ask you this question: Before you came to The Hague for these proceedings, did you ever see that document that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now finally, I'd ask that the witness be shown document -- sorry, Exhibit 150, and again a hard copy will be provided to the witness. Your Honours, the document to be shown on this occasion is a document we have been referring to in this trial as the Zejnilagic order which was the subject of analysis on a previous occasion with another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'll just ask you to look at that document. Do you have in front of you a document which is dated the 15th of September 1993, and is an order to attack, which is ultimately signed by Enver Zejnilagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to take you to a couple of aspects -- I should ask -- before I take you to aspects, I'll just ask you the question. Before you came to The Hague for the purpose of these proceedings, had you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just going to ask -- well, before I ask you, I should ask you this: With your -- the military background that you had, are you in a position to offer professional comments about the structure of a military order, if you were asked those questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That puts an end to that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I would like to give a comment, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If you have a comment, you feel free. Unless the Prosecution objects to the comment, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I would like to make a comment regarding this order. I see that it is dated the 15th of September, which is totally illogical because after the 13th, which is when we were not successful in Crni Vrh, and after the 14th, after Uzdol, there was such a disappointment among people that nobody did anything. Therefore, I do not understand who wrote this on the 15th, because it was my impression that there was no activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to have a look at paragraph number 4 of this order. Do you have that paragraph there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you just look at the last couple of sections and just read those out? Obviously you're reading in the Bosnian language but do you see it says -- sorry, I take that back. I'll read it to you. Do you see the passage where it says, "Combat disposition, forces to create conditions for the attack by the main forces, forces of the first echelon support and reserve forces ready for attack at 0600 hours on the 16th of September 1993. Command post to be in the Voljevac sector." Do you see that section there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, thanks. And could I just ask you also to look at one other part I would just like to show you about this. Could you look at paragraph 9, please which has got the heading, "Intelligence support."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So do you see there where it says, "In the course of 15 September 1993, all units shall send IP, reconnaissance patrols, and IG, reconnaissance groups, to reconnoitre the axis of attack against the enemy." Do you see those passages there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I fully understand what you said earlier on. Were you aware yourself of any such combat activity taking place early on the 16th in the Blace area and in particular on the axis described in paragraph 2 here, the Zgon-Sljeme-Makljen axis. I'm talking now about your personal recollection. Do you remember any such action taking place there on the 16th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: All I remember is -- on the 16th most likely, is that a small group tried to reach Crni Vrh. They were not successful. They came back quite soon thereafter. And all of that had no impact basically. Therefore, I do not remember any significant military activity after the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And even including this small and unsuccessful one that you've just referred to, after that, was there any offensive combat activity whatsoever in that area, to your recollection, for the next two months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
