utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Perhaps those documents could be returned now and I'm going to move on to another sequence of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could the witness please be shown Exhibit 159. I'll provide a hard copy of this. Your Honours, just while the witness is looking at that, could I just ask when it would be appropriate, when Your Honours would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you have in front of you there a document dated the 16th of the 9th, which is an inquiry by Stjepan Siber, deputy commander of the Bosnian army, directed to the 6th Corps, concerning the events in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, firstly, as a matter of specifics, did you yourself ever see that document before you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were you yourself aware that Stjepan Siber was making that inquiry on the 16th of the 9th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. I wasn't. I did know that there was someone asking questions but I didn't know who precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you've indicated that your own direct commander, Enver Buza, made inquiries of you. Did he tell you who was asking him questions from higher up the chain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't remember him telling me the specific name. That was certainly not customary. He would usually say, I want to speak to the corps, or I want to speak to Sarajevo, but you would usually not specify the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown another document now. This one is Exhibit 227, and we'll provide a hard copy of it to the witness. Your Honours, the document to be shown now is a document dated 16th of September, 1993, and it's an inquiry directed by Jusuf Jasarevic, who was the head of the military security in Sarajevo at that time down the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So do you have in front of you now a document dated the 16th of the 9th from Jusuf Jasarevic directed to the military security service of the 6th Corps concerning the reports of a massacre of Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before, but I assume this must have been the reason why we were getting calls from the corps all the time urging us on to compile the report as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Can you recall now whether or not you personally were told that Jusuf Jasarevic was making these inquiries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. I didn't even know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just indicate that on list of documents that was circulated there were two other similar documents from that person but in light of the witness's answer, that's 228 and 229, I'm not going to put those to him. Very well. There is an another document I would seek to be shown now and that is document number 232, and I would ask that a hard copy of that be shown to the witness, please. We have it. Your Honours, the first page is just a title page and so it needs to be turned over to the second page in both the English and the Bosnian. Actually in the English page -- I apologise for that. That's the case in Bosnian. In the English translation there is some text in the first page and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would just ask you to read that text, please. And then I'll ask you some questions. Very well, sorry. Have you had the chance to read that now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before you came to The Hague, had you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Having regard to the contends of the information in that document, do you say that that information there is consistent or inconsistent with the results of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I see that this report was based on Buza's report. After Buza's report was compiled, I helped, based on such information as I had. But I don't remember some of these things being part of my original investigation or findings, such as the number of casualties or the emphasis that is placed on women with weapons. I don't remember having come across these things myself during my investigation. However, as to the fact that everyone was armed and the fact that their artillery had caused the best part of the devastation, that certainly holds true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And finally, could the witness be shown Exhibit 236. And a hard copy will be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I just ask you to take a moment to read the text of 236 and just -- just tell us when you've finished reading it and then I'll ask you some brief questions about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before you came to The Hague for these proceedings, had you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Don't remember having seen this before, but I am familiar with its substance and it reflects my own feelings when I carried out an investigation. What I felt and found at the time was quite similar. This is perhaps a slightly more detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There is only one detail I would ask you about. It mentions the name there of Slavko Mendes and you mentioned earlier on in your --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Mendes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mendes. Please forgive my pronunciation. But you mentioned the a soldier who had been captured and taken up towards the school but who had then been shot. Is that the person that you were referring to at that time or is it somebody different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think it's Slavko Mendes. However, my information on how he was killed was different. They walked into a school and they made him walk in front so he could call on the others to surrender. Once he opened the door to the classroom in which the soldiers were billeted, they shot at him and killed him. So that is the one detail that constitutes the discrepancy between the two accounts. But I don't have a particularly fresh recollection. I did know this person well, however, Slavko Mendes, so that's why I remember the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have much to go but it might be appropriate to take the break now and it will allow me to as the remaining questions in a very short order when we finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will take the break now and we will resume at quarter to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Just there is now a final few questions. There is some that just concern the beginnings of this investigation. Sorry, pardon me, I've lost the text. You indicated that at first, you simply asked some questions for your own information from Osman Hero. At the time when you asked those questions for information, at that stage, were you aware of any allegation of the massacre of civilians in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. However, after that, there came a time when formal statements came to be taken. And I just want to ask you, what was the need to take formal statements? Or what triggered -- perhaps I'll put the question another way. What triggered the need to take formal statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: My first interview with Osman Hero was initiated by Hero himself. I think he had a need to tell his story. He was having a hard time. It wasn't really a need to draw up a formal statement. I just wanted to take down what he was telling me. I could see that he was having a hard time and that he had the need to tell someone about this. Probably he had done something that was not in keeping with his own moral standards. I realised that those were actually statements being taken when I went into Erzimana's office and I saw Jusuf Hero right there but I can't remember specifically whether it was the same day or the next day. At any rate, Erzimana told me to stay and to listen to the interview. She said there was a report to compile. I still didn't realise what it was about but I just sat there and I listened to what he was saying. I was taking notes. It was only a day or two later that there were public announcements of a massacre. It was only then that it dawned on me that statements should be drawn up about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And -- yes, thank you for that. Now, I just have a series of concluding questions. You made reference in your evidence to an institution called the Vakuf Brigade and I wanted to ask you, do you remember the number of that brigade, what its brigade number was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think the 305th, possibly the 317th, something like that. I know that there was a 305th. I'm not sure if that was the one, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When you're talking about the Vakuf Brigade, can you remember the name of the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think it was Zejnilagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When you saw President Izetbegovic on that occasion at the end of September, did he make any suggestion to you that further investigation was warranted or required?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, in a way. He scolded us for creating a problem, saying that it would take a lot of time to clear things up, to show that things were not like that. I understood from the -- his general points that he would remain adamant that further reports, more precise reports, be made, although it had been my opinion all along that it wasn't like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were any -- to your knowledge, were any further such reports made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We did compile a number of reports. I can't remember how many. As for the corps level, or other high level bodies, I really have no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And with respect to those reports, can you indicate if not the precise date, approximately the range of months over when -- weeks or months over when those reports were made and who they were made to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think it wasn't until three or four or five days had gone by that we sent the first report via Paket communications to the 6th Corps. Clarifications were requested later on so we sent further reports. It's just I can't remember exactly how much time had gone by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Can you indicate whether or not the subsequent reports and subsequent clarifications went on through the month of October and into November or whether it was all wrapped up within a few weeks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I really can't be very specific but I think it may have been by the beginning of October. But I can't really be specific about this. I'm just unsure as to how long it took altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And finally, at around the time of the 16th, you indicated a small action which took place on the 16th of September, after which there was no -- I think you've answered that question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the end of the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is, Your Honours. Could I ask for a brief break for a few moments? There are several matters which have been raised as recently as a few moments ago but have greatly taken the Prosecution by surprise. I just need to check several matters which I need to put to the witness. I don't necessarily need Your Honours to leave court. It will take me three, four, five minutes to find the information I need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness J. My name is David Re. I'm representing the Prosecution here and I'm going to ask you some questions about your testimony. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, please if you don't understand anything I say or you need clarification, don't hesitate to ask. I want to make sure we understand each other very clearly and correctly in this questioning, okay? In your evidence earlier, you said that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. In your evidence earlier this afternoon, you said that your information told you that the artillery, the HVO artillery, caused most of the devastation, including the deaths of anyone who was in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just make sure. If my learned friend is going to put a conclusion like that it will have to come directly from the transcript because I don't think that was the import of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Earlier you said that the HVO artillery caused most of the devastation in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that they produced the most of devastation. I said that among other causes of devastation was their action as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You of course didn't visit the scene, did you, afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't perform any crime-scene analysis, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't perform any crater analysis, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We had no access to the area. Therefore, your questions are not pertinent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't actually see any Croatian artillery or HVO artillery yourself in Uzdol, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. However, over the radio, when our radio officer managed to intercept their radio communications, we heard them talking among themselves and cursing at each other for the friendly fire that had killed some of their persons, and that was the basis for our conclusion about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please turn on the other microphone as well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll move it. Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the question directed to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you first talk to Defence investigators about this matter, Witness J?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Perhaps some 10 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you tell the Defence about this, that you overheard something on HVO radio communications? The reason I ask this, Witness J, is that learned Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We don't mind what the reason is and we don't want speeches to be made. If he's got a question that can be asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question and put it in another form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Over the last two days, Defence counsel, that is Mr. Morrissey and Mr. Mettraux, Witness J, have provided us with what are called proofing notes or a witness statement of what you were going to say in court today. The information you provided just then and earlier about your overhearing HVO communications about friendly fire is not in those proofing notes. It's not in the information the Defence provided to the Prosecution yesterday or last week. When did you tell Defence about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I object to the form of that question. The speech that was contained before the question is highly misleading, as my learned friend well knows. I don't want to make a speech about whether it was communicated to the Prosecutors. But my learned friend knows very well that -- well, I think I have to say it now, actually. It's up to the Court whether I say it in front of the witness or not. But this was communicated and if you need me to go on, I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since this was communicated, I don't think there is any objections on your side. Because the Prosecution is entitled to ask about this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I absolutely agree that the question at line 15 and 16 is unobjectionable and can be asked. But the speech that came before it I object to, and I've got my reasons for objecting to it. I don't object to the question. I'm objecting to the speech. And perhaps just the question on its own could be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Re, you may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand which part I have to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just leave out the first part and I believe that question is permissible. You may directly ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The information you provided is not in the proofing notes which were provided yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to this. It doesn't matter for Mr. Re to make speeches to the witness. He's allowed to ask him the question. The witness can give an answer. That's what has to happen in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's no different, Your Honour with respect, by saying you provided a statement on such-and-such a day, on the 1st of June, then on the 3rd of June, and the information you gave is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see there is no difference. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Understand the question, Witness J. The information you have just given the Court wasn't in proofing notes provided yesterday or in a statement provided by the Defence to us last week. When did you tell the Defence about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think that I remembered that yesterday and I did so subsequently, after our conversation. This was the detail that I remembered after we concluded our conversation, and it seemed important to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Back in 1992, you I think you said you were imprisoned firstly by the Croatian authorities for a lengthy period and then you were re-imprisoned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The situation was that you and your family had suffered at HVO hands, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You'd suffered very badly, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We suffered to an average extent. Some people suffered more than us, some suffered less.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, you lost your house, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Partially. Not my house but, rather, my father's.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm having difficulty getting sound. Could you just bear with me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, the situation was that three members of your family lost houses in a row, didn't they? That was you and your two brothers. And as a result, you were homeless.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence earlier was that you had nowhere to live when you joined the Prozor Independent Battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I had no funds because part of my house that had burned down was the part where I had money and food. I need to clarify something here. It was only my brother's apartment that was destroyed in fire. However, my apartment within that house was fine, was inhabitable. The danger that threatened us did not come from ordinary people but, rather, from the criminals who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: And thugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you were captured by the Croatian or Herceg-Bosna authorities, they in fact put you on trial. They took you to a court, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: An attempt was made to put me on trial. However, the trial was concluded after it was established that there were no witnesses and no evidence to substantiate their charges against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They charged you with what could loosely be termed a rebellion, joining a rebellion against the Croatian or the Croat Herceg-Bosna authorities, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I have to clarify that. The HVO as a military formation and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fought together up until October of 1992. When the agreement was reached, and I don't know details about this, but later on it was written in various sources of information that an agreement was made between the Croatian side and the Serbian side, Prozor became Croatian territory. So the inhabitants who did not want to live under the Croatian rule carried out an attack and defeated the part of the Bosnian army and all residents fit for military service were incarcerated in camps. This is how I ended up in a camp. There were about 5.000 to 6.000 inmates in the camp. Later on, they had to explain how that came about, because the Bosniaks and the Croats in the Prozor area used to get along extremely well. I myself had a lot of friends among Croats. Therefore, they had to find a justification for all of this, and they came up with a group of extremists, as they called them, who allegedly urged people to rebel. This is how they identified a group of about 20 people comprising the most intelligent and the most educated people who allegedly led the rebellion. I was among them. And we were tried as the leaders of an alleged rebellion. And that was a total nonsense. There was no rebellion and there was nothing to rebel against.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you and the others mistreated while you were in HVO custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. I was fortunate enough to encounter once again my students who had a lot of respect for me, brought me cigarettes and treated me decently. I had no unpleasant experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were other detainees taken from that camp and used by the HVO as human shields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Not at the time. That was the first camp that was established in October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the second one you were in? Was that the same camp or a different one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: After the conflict between the BH army and the HVO, which was in fact the first conflict in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for another year or so the BH army and the HVO were together in almost all areas. That means that that conflict was ironed out and that was done by the new year. Nothing really changed except that the power in town was taken over by the HVO. After June of 1993, when the conflicts between the BH army and the HVO escalated in other areas, as a preventive measure they started arresting Bosniak civilians. First only small numbers of them, so that I, together with another 20 or 30 people, was incarcerated in a facility near police station. Later on, we were taken to the nuclear shelter near a factory. That happened in June of 1993. However, already in July of 1993, mass arrests started and were concluded sometime in August, when the entire male population was arrested and sent to the camps in Herzegovina and elsewhere. Some of them were kept in Prozor, whereas those who were not fit for military service were deported. The ones who remained in Prozor at the time were housed in several camps. One was at the school centre, the other one was at the TO warehouse, the military police facilities and so on. There were five or six such locations. The inmates were used as labour force; on one occasion they were used as human shields. However, I myself did not experience this because in late June I was released from prison and as I was aware of the looming danger - there had already been murders committed by criminals with a criminal record and thugs - I, as a result of that, fled to the territory under the command -- under the control of the BH army. That's my story.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Look, as a result of your imprisonment by the HVO twice and the loss of your house, is it fair to say that you were not well-disposed to the HVO and those forces in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: You are not right. I gave an interview to a journalist upon reaching the free territory, and everything I said there is contrary to what you are alleging. I said that everything that was going on had not been planned by local Croats. The orders had come from outside and local Croats simply had to implement it. I did not change my opinion about the local Croats. I continue to see these people to this day. However, as for those who had committed crimes, the situation is different there. I see what you're trying to do. You're trying to show that everything I'm doing now is a result of the hatred I feel. That's not true. To this day, one of my best friends is an HVO commander from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there members of the Prozor Independent Battalion, in which you served, who had also been imprisoned by the HVO and Herceg-Bosna authorities, merely because they were a male of military service -- sorry, military age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What percentage of those in the Prozor Independent Battalion had been imprisoned by the HVO or Herceg-Bosna authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I couldn't say, but quite a large number, because many of those who were forced to work, upon fleeing had no choice but join the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were some of those members of the Prozor Independent Battalion who had been imprisoned, had they been used as human shields by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Perhaps that was the case. However, I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about their being used for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: By the HVO. Like, for example, had any of them been taken for trench-digging on the front lines or that type of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. Those civilians who were imprisoned in Prozor were used as a labour force, working on fortifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not challenging what you said about your having no ill feelings towards the local Croats, but in the group amongst the Prozor Independent Battalion, it would be fair to say, wouldn't it, there were some soldiers there who weren't as well-disposed towards the local Croats as you were? Some of them, I'm suggesting, bore real antipathy towards the Croats because of what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that question has to be clarified because the question is was the antipathy towards the local Croats or towards the Croats generally, which my learned friend put in the second part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, if you could, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I mean local Croats.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It is understandable that some of the people were bitter, but those were individual cases. People who had suffered certain mistreatment and had animosity towards them. However, in general terms, it is hard to draw such a conclusion. Once again, I will repeat that the relations between Croats and Bosniaks were excellent. They were on a very high level. Therefore, I was surprised that something like that happened, regardless of the orders coming from above. Let me just add to something I have already stated. When I was in camp, I went to dig. I dug in front line, at the front line, which was very dangerous. The HVO policemen escorting me started crying and said, "I can do nothing to help you but give you cigarettes and beer." Similarly, the president of the municipality, who was representing the HVO, was a colleague of mine, who said to me, "I'm sorry, I can't help you at all. This has to do with higher politics, and we have no influence over that." I'm saying this just to explain to you what was the interethnic relationship like, and this was completely outside of the higher political forces who produced all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Just confining ourselves at the moment to those in the Prozor Independent Battalion, you said that some people had suffered certain mistreatment and had animosity towards the local Croats. Some of those people were those who took part in the attack on Uzdol, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It's a possibility. I have no information to show that, though. Nor did anyone look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From your position within the Prozor Independent Battalion, were you involved in the planning, the preplanning, of the attack on Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you in the communications centre while the attack was taking place on the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm not sure where you get this at all, that I was at the communications centre. It's a small hut, the command. Everything was there, virtually everything. So being there, you're in all of these places at the same time, in a manner of speaking. At that point in time, I had no specific duty. Therefore, I could not have been officially party to any preparations, nor was I aware of any plans or what would be happening. I can only draw conclusions based on conversations that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm actually asking you where you were on the 14th. Could you describe this hut? Where was this hut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was at Dobro Polje. It's a wooden hut, a cottage, that was used in peace time by people who worked in the forest, who chopped the trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was in this hut? What was it equipped with during this period of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: There was virtually nothing. There were two or three rooms. We made our own beds to lie on. There was the occasional table and chair. The only thing we had, aside from that building, was a small shed where the radio equipment was kept. So we decided to call this communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You had a radio equipment. What about weaponry? Was weaponry kept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. We had no weapons to begin with. We had no weapons to keep in a storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What other equipment did you have besides radio equipment? I mean, what other material or what things were in this headquarters or communication centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Next to nothing. There was a cabinet containing some files. It was a metal cabinet. There was some radio equipment at the communications centre and later on, we got a computer which we used to work Paket communications. And that was all that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you get the computer, relative to the attack on Uzdol? Was it before or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can't remember, really. I think it was later. It was afterwards. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have a telephone in this hut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: A field telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about electricity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Generator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who operated from that hut? Or who was based there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Members of the battalion for the most part who weren't locals. That was the only place they could sleep. The remaining soldiers would go back home to spend the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's in their villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. Those who were locals from those villages, or those who came from outside but had relatives around the area would sleep there. Those of us who had no one in the area would sleep in the cottage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Enver Buza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: He slept there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he based there? Is that where he spent his day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That was the only place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that where Mr. Halilovic came for the meeting? Was that the place in Dobro Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's the distance between Dobro Polje and Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: About ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you see Uzdol from Dobro Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There were three units which participated in the attack on Uzdol from the Prozor Independent Battalion, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can't remember how many or which specific units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just going back to the hut for a moment, did the hut have military maps in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We had next to nothing, not that I saw any equipment lying around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking about maps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Not that I can remember seeing any. Perhaps there were maps. It's just that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just going to show you a large map which is on a board which my colleague has. It's called Operation Neretva. It's a copy of it. Was this map -- I think it's D231 -- was that map in the hut in Dobro Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Never seen this one before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to the transcript to reveal that that's just a copy of the exhibit. The real map has been tendered. If the Prosecutor wants to go down this path, he should show the real map and not that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The record actually does reflect it's a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think up to now there is no dispute over this map, whether it's original or it's a copy. To me there is no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, I said 231. I meant actually 131 for the record. Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness J, there were three units within the Prozor Independent Battalion which led the attack, and they were firstly led by Sefik Corbadzic [phoen], secondly by Osman Hero and thirdly by Eniz Hujdur. Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to that. It's got two parts to it. The witness has not agreed there were three units involved in the attack. He was specifically asked and he specifically said he doesn't know. So the Prosecutor can't build into the question. He can ask whether those individuals led companies, or break up the question in any way he wishes but he can't have the first part as a given because the witness said specifically he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's cross-examination. I'm suggesting to the witness that's what happened. He can agree or disagree or say he doesn't know. He can answer in whatever way he likes. It's my proposition I'm putting to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's perfectly permissible. There were three units and they were led by these three people. What do you say to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The witness may not be a military person, so maybe he doesn't know about how many units are there. You could ask the question one by one, first to establish whether the witness knows there are three units in that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness J, I'm suggesting there were three units which -- from the Prozor Independent Battalion which participated in the attack on Uzdol. What can you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't know. Nor did I ever have a chance to find out who was involved. Nor was I interested. I know that it was decided who would be going. How exactly the decision was taken is something that I can't speak about. I know the battalion only had four companies. Now, what the subdivision of that was is something I have no idea about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that in your speaking to up to a hundred people in the days or weeks after the attack on Uzdol, you never found out how many units were participating in the attack? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That was completely irrelevant. Those were small units. These units probably had names but I didn't understand much about that. Where necessary, people simply shifted from one unit to a different unit, depending on what was the closest place to spend the night. So those were no fixed units set in stone. I considered all those persons to be battalion members and I asked no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said you weren't interested. You mean you weren't interested when you spoke to the hundred or so people, up to a hundred people in the days and weeks after the attack on Uzdol, as to who had led specific units of men? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He didn't say that and that's a misleading way of putting the question, Your Honour. If you look back to the situation where he said "nor was I interested," he was asked the question at line 6, Your Honours, page 76: "Q. I'm suggesting to you that there were three units which -- from the Prozor Independent Battalion which participated in the an attack on Uzdol. What can you say to that?" And the witness said, "A. I don't know. Nor did I ever have a chance to find out who was involved. Nor was I interested." In other words, he said "nor was I interested" in respect of a specific question and my friend is now in my respectful submission distorting that answer in cross-examination in an impermissible way, as you can see from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The objection is impermissible. The objection is improper. I'm entitled to put to the witness a reason, based on what he said, for why he was not interested -- why he didn't explore it with these people. He said he wasn't interested. I'm asking him is the reason why you didn't try to find out who were the leaders of the units is that you were not interested? Is that what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe just put a very simple question. Ask him what he was not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I need to establish whether he was interested. If I can be permitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to establish what he's not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have to make sure, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that you don't know how many units participated in the attack on Uzdol, you didn't have a chance to find out who was involved, and "nor was I interested." I'm asking you, during the period in which you took statements from people or spoke to a hundred people, up to a hundred people, after the attack, were you not interested in finding out who the commanders of the units participating in the attack were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Those were no commanders at all. Nor did I know that anyone had a duty to lead a group. All I knew was there were four companies that were part of that battalion. It struck me as logical at the time that company commanders would lead their own men but this is not something that I pondered at the time. Nor would I be inclined to assume now that some people had special assignments and were in charge of a special group of men. When I talked to these people, I didn't notice that to be a substantial factor. There was a group of people who left. Their commander was Buza. I spared no thought to their inferiors or subordinate commanders. Could have been platoon commanders, whatever. There should have been about ten squads, I think. So this is a detail easily overlooked. I am not familiar with this sort of background. Nor would it have meant anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it a situation of don't ask, don't tell? I mean, when you were talking to these up to a hundred people afterwards, you didn't ask, and they didn't tell you, whether there were company commanders involved in the attack on Uzdol or who -- if there were, who they were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: For me, there was only one group. This group was given the assignment of taking part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of these, as you said, up to 100 people, did they all participate in the attack on Uzdol? That's why you were talking to them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, yes. I wanted to find out what exactly had happened, and that was the reason I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, did all 100 or up to 100 participate in the attack on Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I am really not positive about the number of people who participated but I never said that I talked to a hundred different people. May have been the case but I don't remember the specific figure. That's all I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The people you spoke to, or decided to speak to, you decided to speak to because they had participated in the attack on Uzdol; is that correct? However many it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: At first, I talked to people out of sheer curiosity, my curiosity. Later on, I was given an assignment. I was told that I should help compile a report, and this report was to be compiled by interviewing individuals who were involved in the attack. That was the reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: -- I interviewed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you find or select these people? Were there names on a list of those who had gone into battle on the 14th of September or was it just known who was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: People recounted what happened to someone else. Everybody had a story to tell, something that they saw or experienced. I would stick around, as they were talking I was on the lookout for elements for my own story, and when a story struck me as particularly interesting, I would call the person and ask them a number of questions in order to create a fuller picture of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean for your own story? Was it for your own diary or record you were keeping for your own purposes or what? I just want to know what you mean by your own story.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. No. There has been a misunderstanding. I meant what I was tasked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What you just said, you would "stick around" as people were talking and "I was on the lookout for elements for my own story, and when a story struck me as particularly interesting, I would call the person and ask them a number of questions", is that what you were tasked to do? Stick around listening to people talking and then follow up stories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No one specified how I should do it. Alongside with everyone else I was merely requested to compile a report on what had happened. Each had their own method. Mine was to listen to people's conversations and glean what I believed was important, and thus help compile this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who else was -- I said -- I withdraw that. You said "alongside with everyone else." Who was the "everyone else" you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, Erzimana, who was officially assistant commander for intelligence, and Mustafa Bektas, who was assistant commander for security. I helped these people out. That was my duty. But they were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Erzimana Dzogic, is that the person we are talking about, or Dzogic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: She gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 22nd of May 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to this. Your Honours, it's not proper for the Prosecutor to go putting slabs of a statement from somebody who was never called by the Prosecution to give evidence at this Tribunal to this witness. That would be highly improper. There is another reason why it would be highly improper and it -- there is a number of reasons why. I'll go into them in detail if needs be. But at the moment I'll contend myself with this: She exists; they didn't call her. This statement should not be allowed to be put on to the record in any way, nor should it be allowed to be put to this witness. If the Prosecution wanted to call her, they had their chance, and this is now an attempt, in my submission, to put something on the record which is highly unreliable and ought not to be used. Could I just make the comment that the Defence, of course, themselves -- I don't want to go on now the witness is here. Could this matter perhaps be put on hold briefly until there is a break and then I can raise it and discuss it properly with the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe that's a good suggestion. We will stop here for today and we'll resume tomorrow morning, and in the morning, Mr. Morrissey should furnish us with more reasons on this aspect. We might have a small debate on that before we continue with the cross-examination of this witness. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just indicate for the record now that the Prosecution's present intention from this witness's evidence would be to call rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are not going to deal with it until we finished this witness. Well, Witness, I have to give you some advice that I did with other witnesses. That is, since you came to The Hague, you are still under the oath. So do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your evidence. You understand that? We have to stop today and we'll continue tomorrow. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And since we don't have another witness for tomorrow, we will start at 10.00 in the morning. So, Witness, see you at 10.00 tomorrow morning in the same courtroom. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, 7 July, 2005, at 10.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.56 p.m.,
